title: How Nuclear Missile Officers Eat & Sleep 60 Feet Underground
asof: Figures from US Air Force & National Park Service, as of 2026 · sources in description

shots.s: Two officers ride an elevator sixty feet down.
At the bottom, a blast door weighing eight tons.
Behind it, a capsule the size of a bedroom.
For the next twenty-four hours, this is their whole world.
Their job: watch over ten nuclear missiles.
So how do you eat,
sleep,
and stay sane,
sixty feet underground?
This is Montana.
Open prairie, as far as you can see.
Hidden in it, there are Minuteman Three missiles in silos.
Each one can reach targets more than six thousand miles away.
The US keeps them on alert at three bases,
in Montana, North Dakota and Wyoming.
For every ten missiles,
there's one underground control center.
Above it sits a building that looks like a ranch house.
That's the missile alert facility.
You drive out across the prairie.
Before you go,
you pick up a cooler of food for the site's kitchen.
Then a small elevator takes you down.
Sixty feet.
At the bottom, a steel blast door.
It can only be opened from inside.
A voice inside shouts "clear."
You shout back, and the door swings open.
Nobody can be in here alone.
The Air Force calls it a no-lone zone.
The old crew briefs you face to face.
Then they leave, and the capsule is yours.
The shift is twenty-four hours.
Checks, logs, verifications, over and over.
You watch the status of your missiles.
You check messages,
and track maintenance teams at the silos.
If a motion sensor trips at a silo, you send security.
One officer called it a very repetitive job.
That's the point, he said.
If a launch order ever came,
two people would have to turn two keys.
They're placed so far apart that one person can't turn both.
A former missileer described the job
as hours and hours of sheer boredom,
punctuated by seconds of panic.
There's no kitchen down here.
Upstairs, a missile chef cooks for everyone on site.
Security forces, the facility manager, and you.
One chef, working alone,
for ten to twenty people at a site.
You order from a menu before going down.
Then the chef brings it to you at set times.
For a lot of crews,
that's the only face they see all day.
There's one bed.
Two people.
So you take turns.
One sleeps, the other stays awake at the console.
There's always someone watching.
A small sleeping area, and the hum of machines.
And there's a toilet, in a capsule built for two.
No phones.
No personal computers.
One officer's niece was born while he was on alert.
He didn't find out until later.
The walls are covered in notes and drawings,
from crews going back to the 1990s.
Generations of missileers,
telling the next crew they're not alone.
Some officers pull this shift eight times a month.
Morning. The new crew rides down.
Face-to-face handover.
Then the door, the elevator,
and sixty feet up to the prairie.
Since 1962, crews have stood this watch.
The goal isn't to use the missiles, one officer said.
It's to be so ready that they never have to be tested.
Could you spend twenty-four hours in that room?
